depth.correction: Equal-precedence operations must preserve left-to-right grouping. For 3 + 4 * 2, the operator stack holds + then *; final popping emits 3 4 2 * +. For 8 / 2 + 3, / is emitted before +. An opening parenthesis is a barrier until its matching close.
depth.misconception: “Equal precedence implies the right operator runs first”

title: Shunting-Yard Parsing: When to Use It

writing.exampleCaption: Complete std-only expression-shunting-yard program for its typed teaching fixture. Parsing and output construction are separate from the core algorithm.
writing.explanation:
For 3 + 4 * 2, the operator stack holds + then *; final popping emits 3 4 2 * +. For 8 / 2 + 3, / is emitted before +. An opening parenthesis is a barrier until its matching close.

The worked program is a complete executable for this pattern. Its core function uses typed input so the state transitions remain visible. The challenge input contract is: Convert the infix expression to postfix tokens. The visible fixture is `3 + 4 * 2` and its example result is `3 4 2 * +`. The implementation and additional semantic fixtures were checked against an independent reference calculation. Those bounded tests establish these examples; they are not a proof for all inputs or a measurement on an iPhone.

Return a canonical String from solve: lowercase true/false for booleans; decimal integers without extra signs, leading zeros or whitespace; comma-separated sequence values and semicolon-separated groups. Whole-number medians have no decimal suffix; half medians use .5. Do not append a newline to the returned value. Preserve the explicitly named textual sentinels such as none or #. Input fixtures are bounded so the demonstrated arithmetic fits its named Rust types; satisfy the stated input preconditions before applying the algorithm.

String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

A problem is a good match for Shunting-Yard Parsing when it asks for infix parsing and calculator implementations. Here the concrete task is: Convert the infix expression to postfix tokens. The visible input `3 + 4 * 2` is an example, not a definition of the whole problem. Ask what operations the solution must support and what the input guarantees. Look for nested structure, next-greater relationships, or ordered processing. A plain scan is enough when no unresolved state must be retained. The right choice follows from those guarantees, not from a familiar noun in the prompt.

The decisive invariant is: Use an operator stack to emit operations only when precedence and associativity allow. Try to say why it applies to the task without quoting the implementation. Which fact becomes known after one update, and which possible answers remain? A stack remembers unfinished work in last-in-first-out order; a queue processes work in first-in-first-out order. Say what each stored item still needs. If that claim cannot be maintained on a legal input, the pattern is wrong or one of its preconditions is missing. A counterexample is more useful than a vague warning: change one property of the sample, trace the first two steps, and identify the exact claim that fails.

Compare costs before committing. The advertised bound is O(n) time · O(n) space; identify the operation responsible for it and the extra memory it needs. Then compare a straightforward alternative: a direct scan, full sort, or repeated recomputation may be easier but can pay for the same work many times. Do not choose the more elaborate method just because it has a famous name. For the sample, predict `3 4 2 * +` and explain which part of the state lets the method reach that result.

When the prompt is ambiguous, ask about input size, ordering, duplicates, and required output format. Check empty containers, one item, repeated equal values, and the work left in the structure after the input ends. `Vec` works as a stack; `VecDeque` supplies efficient operations at both ends. Avoid removing from the front of a `Vec` in a long loop. The Rust sketch can show a useful primitive without proving that the whole task is solved; connect each primitive to the requested output. You should be able to name a fitting case, a near miss, and the assumption separating them before writing the first line.
